nameStory: The rock gunnel gets its name from its long, slender body shape that resembles an old-fashioned gunnel - the upper edge of a ship's side. The 'rock' part comes from its habit of hiding among rocky crevices and under stones in the intertidal zone. Some folks also call it 'butterfish' because of its incredibly slippery, mucus-covered skin that makes it slip through your fingers like butter!
description: The rock gunnel is a long, eel-like fish that looks almost snake-like as it weaves through tide pools and rocky shallows. This slender fish typically grows 6-12 inches long and has a continuous dorsal fin running along most of its back like a ribbon. Its body is covered in tiny scales and a thick layer of slippery mucus that helps it squeeze into tight rocky crevices. Rock gunnels come in various earth tones - brown, olive, or reddish - often with darker mottling that helps them blend perfectly with seaweed and rocks.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely elongated and eel-like with a compressed, ribbon-thin profile that feels firm yet flexible when handled - like a thick rubber band

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long, continuous dorsal fin runs along the back with distinctive dark eyespots (10-14 spots) that look like a row of watching eyes

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Incredibly slippery and slimy to touch due to thick mucus coating - will slip right out of your hands like wet soap

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Variable earth tones from brown to olive-green or reddish, often with darker mottled patterns that match surrounding seaweed and rocks

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small terminal mouth (at the tip of the snout) with tiny teeth, designed for picking small prey from rock crevices

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 6-12 inches long but appears much longer due to its thin, stretched-out proportions

habitat: Rock gunnels live in the rocky intertidal zone along New England's coast, especially areas with lots of seaweed, barnacles, and mussels. You'll find them hiding under rocks, in tide pools, or squeezed into narrow crevices between boulders when the tide goes out. They prefer areas with good wave action and rocky substrate rather than sandy or muddy bottoms.

seasonality.spring: Spawning season begins - look for adults gathering in deeper tide pools and under larger rocks. Fish may appear slightly more colorful during breeding.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easiest to find during low tides. Adults and juveniles hide under rocks and in crevices - lift rocks gently to spot them coiled underneath.
seasonality.fall: Still common in tide pools but may move to slightly deeper water. Good time to observe them as they're often well-fed and robust before winter.
seasonality.winter: Move to deeper water or lower intertidal zones. Less commonly seen during tide pool exploration, but still present under larger, more stable rocks.

funFact: Rock gunnels can actually tie themselves in knots! When threatened or trying to wedge into an impossibly tight crevice, they'll literally tie their flexible body into a knot and then untie themselves - a ability shared with very few fish species in the world.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small eels, but rock gunnels have that distinctive row of dark eyespots along their dorsal fin that eels lack. Remember: 'Eyes on the ridge, it's a gunnel you've bridge!' - meaning if you see those eyespots along the back fin, you've found a gunnel, not an eel.
contextualKnowledge: Don't be confused by the alternate name 'butterfish' - there's also a completely different deep-water species called butterfish (Peprilus triacanthus) that's rounder and silvery. The rock gunnel earned this nickname purely from its slippery texture, not any relation to the other butterfish.
compareHints: Rock gunnels are the only gunnel species commonly found in New England tide pools, making identification easier. They're most similar to small eels or snake blennies, but the rock gunnel's distinctive row of dark eyespots along the dorsal fin and extremely slimy texture sets it apart from any other elongated fish you'll find in the intertidal zone.
